newsitem.title: USA: AISI president says steel imports "discouraging".
newsitem.headline: AISI president says steel imports "discouraging".

text.p: The level of steel imports entering the U.S. market so far this year is "discouraging" and may be on track to set an annual record, the president of the American Iron and Steel Institute said.

"The (import) numbers now are discouraging, and I think it's only because we've had such a strong (domestic) steel market that (North American) steel companies have been able to maintain profitability," Andrew Sharkey, AISI president, told Reuters in an interview.

The AISI is the Washington-based trade group representing North American steel producers. The organization's functions, among other things, include lobbying for the steel industry on Capitol Hill and developing new markets for steel.
According to the most recent Commerce Department data, steel imports in the first four months of '97 totaled almost 11 million tons, up 37.6 percent from the same period last year.
"Annualized, that's a 33 million ton import year, which you know is huge," Sharkey said. "Last year was a little over 29 million tons and that was a record."

Sharkey said much of the foreign material is being offered at prices far below domestic market prices. The domestic steel market is typically one of the world's strongest, and when foreign economies are sluggish the import level usually rises.

The response by North American producers has often been filing trade suits against foreign companies, a tactic that has sometimes soured ongoing negotiations between governments to reach a worldwide steel trade agreement.

"I don't know anybody who sees litigation as where you want to be long term, but by the same token when you look at the nature of the (import) problem...some action has to be taken," Sharkey said. "It does little good to grow the market through all of our (development) programs and then find it's being absorbed by product that's being dumped in this market."
Sharkey said the long-term solution to battling high import levels is for North American producers to continue cutting costs to maintain their global competitiveness.

"But frankly, in the midst of this onslaught, even some of the companies that we know are absolutely the low cost companies are outraged at what's happening here, because it's not based on the law of the market," he said.

Separately, Sharkey said while consolidation is possible in the domestic steel industry during the next several years, he expects to see more partnerships between steel companies, such as in technology or marketing, to keep the industry competitive.

Speculation that U.S. steelmakers will consolidate has been somewhat high in recent months, after the chief executives of some of those companies publicly said they would be interested in merger or acquisition opportunities.

Several companies already have technology partnerships, including USX-U.S. Steel Group and Bethlehem Steel Corp, who formed a joint research agreement a few years ago that enables them to exchange information on iron and steel production.
"I think you're going to see more of that," Sharkey said. "Everybody predicts a lot of consolidation; it's really a cliche.

"Are some companies going to disappear? Sure. Will growth through acquisition be a strategy for some companies? I think there's no question. But I think you're going to see a lot of partnerships, a lot of different combinations."
